title: The Director of 'Kill' Is in Talks to Make a Hollywood Superhero Movie. Two Years Ago, He Couldn't Get a Hindi Film Released.
excerpt: Nikhil Nagesh Bhat went from a stalled career to a TIFF sensation to Universal Studios' shortlist for a superhero franchise. He's also making an action film for Dharma and a Sunny Deol thriller. The Kill effect is real.
body:
In 2022, Nikhil Nagesh Bhat had a film that no one wanted to release. Kill, his ultraviolent action thriller set entirely on a train, had been shot, edited, and shelved. The Indian distributor landscape had no appetite for a Hindi film that looked like a Korean revenge drama and had no A-list star attached.

Then Karan Johar's Dharma Productions picked it up. Then it premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival. Then Lionsgate bought the English-language remake rights. Then it made ₹47 crore against a ₹20 crore budget. And now, in 2026, Nikhil Nagesh Bhat is in active discussions with Universal Studios to direct a Hollywood superhero movie.

This is what a breakout looks like when you're an Indian filmmaker in the global market. It doesn't happen in a straight line. It happens in a violent zigzag.

The Kill Effect

Kill was never supposed to be a crossover hit. It was supposed to be a genre exercise — a single-location action film that tested whether Indian audiences would sit through a film where the protagonist kills 40 people with his bare hands and a railway handbrake. The answer was yes, emphatically, but the real surprise was the international reception.

At TIFF, Kill screened to standing ovations. American critics compared it to The Raid and Train to Busan. Lionsgate moved quickly, announcing a Hollywood remake with Chad Stahelski's 87eleven producing — the same stunt team behind John Wick. The film won Best Male Debut at the Filmfare Awards for Lakshya, and Raghav Juyal's unhinged villain became one of the most talked-about performances of 2024.

For Bhat, the film did something even more valuable than box office returns: it made Hollywood take notice of an Indian director who could do action at a global level.

Universal's Superhero Bet

The details of the Universal Studios project remain under wraps. What's known is that Bhat is in discussions for a superhero film — a genre that has been Hollywood's most lucrative and most creatively embattled territory for the last decade. Marvel's dominance has shown signs of fatigue. DC is rebuilding under James Gunn. Universal, which doesn't have its own superhero franchise, is reportedly looking for fresh voices.

An Indian director with a proven ability to choreograph visceral, grounded action is not an obvious choice for a superhero movie. But it's a smart one. The superhero genre's biggest problem in 2026 is that everything looks the same — the same CGI cityscapes, the same quip-heavy scripts, the same third-act portal in the sky. What Kill proved is that Bhat can make violence feel physical, close, and consequential. That's exactly what a fatigued genre needs.

If the deal closes, Bhat would join a very short list of Indian-origin directors who have helmed major Hollywood studio films. S.S. Rajamouli has been in talks with studios since RRR. Neeraj Pandey has been circling international projects. But a confirmed studio superhero assignment would be a first.

Meanwhile, Back in Mumbai

While Hollywood circles, Bhat isn't waiting. He has two major Indian projects in active development. The first is a mainstream action film for Dharma Productions — the same house that rescued Kill from distribution limbo. The second, announced more recently, is Lakhan, a large-scale action thriller starring Sunny Deol. That film begins shooting in October 2026 and is being positioned as a return to the adrenaline-heavy, crowd-pleasing format that made Deol a household name in the '90s.

For the Indian diaspora, Bhat's trajectory is a familiar pattern with an unfamiliar ending. Indian filmmakers have been doing exceptional work for decades, but Hollywood's doors have historically opened only for actors — and even then, only in supporting roles. The director's chair has remained stubbornly closed. Mira Nair broke through in the indie space. Shekhar Kapur made Elizabeth. But a studio tentpole? That's still uncharted territory.

What It Means for Indian Cinema

The larger story here isn't about one director or one deal. It's about a shift in how Hollywood sources talent. For years, the pipeline ran through film school and the festival circuit — Sundance to a studio development deal. Now, the pipeline increasingly runs through global markets. Rajamouli's RRR changed the calculus. Bhat's Kill confirmed it. The signal to Hollywood is no longer "Indian directors can make art films." It's "Indian directors can make action films that travel."

Whether Bhat's Hollywood project materializes into a greenlit production or stalls in development — as most studio projects do — the fact that he's in the room is the story. Two years ago, he couldn't get a train movie released. Now Universal is asking if he can make people fly.

The Kill effect, as it turns out, isn't just about one film. It's about what happens when the world finally watches what Indian cinema has been capable of all along.
author: Diaspora Desk
